problem: The text says each swapped‑out process is written to a contiguous region of the swap area. In most operating systems the swap image may be stored in non‑contiguous blocks; contiguity is not required.
fix: Replace with: “Each process that is swapped out has its entire address image written to one or more blocks in the swap area; the blocks need not be contiguous.”

problem: The statement “Swap space size is usually a multiple of RAM (e.g., 2× RAM)” is outdated and can mislead students, as modern systems often use smaller or larger swap sizes depending on workload.
fix: Change to: “Swap space size is often chosen as a fraction or multiple of RAM, e.g., 1× to 2× RAM, but the optimal size depends on the workload and system configuration.”

problem: The answer incorrectly assumes that four 10 MB processes can reside in 24 MB of RAM and that three resident processes exist before swapping. In reality only two 10 MB processes (20 MB) can fit; a third process already requires swapping.
fix: Correct answer: “Only two processes can be resident in 24 MB RAM (20 MB used). To run a third (or fifth) 10 MB process, one of the resident processes must be swapped out. Using the longest‑idle policy, swap out the resident process that has been idle the longest, freeing 10 MB for the new process.”
